newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Kohl says budget pact a success, triumph for Waigel.
newsitem.headline: Kohl says budget pact a success, triumph for Waigel.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Saturday a budget pact agreed in Dublin this weekend was a landmark on the way to a stable European currency and a personal triumph for his finance minister, who first proposed the plan.
European Union leaders and their top financial officials on Friday finally agreed a pact to ensure fiscal discipline within economic and monetary union (EMU), ending months of wrangling.
"It is a great success, and a great personal success for Theo Waigel," Kohl told a news conference after the talks.
Waigel first tabled the stability pact a year ago in a bid to reassure both the German public and the inflation-conscious Bundesbank that the future euro would be stable and credible.

Under the terms of the Dublin agreement, those governments which join EMU but then allow their annual budget deficits to exceed three percent of gross domestic product will face sanctions and fines if they fail to take corrective action.
Waigel, who stressed that deterrence was the pact's main purpose, said he was delighted to see how quickly his proposal been given life, even if the talks had been tough.
"This agreement is absolutely decisive for the European currency," he told the news conference. "It lends credibility through supervision, prevention and clear rules."

Germany had often appeared isolated in its demands for the strictest possible terms. France in particular balked at Bonn's wish to deny politicians any major say on whether countries would be punished.
The two countries at the heart of European integration were able to find common ground on the budget pact only with the help of their tiny neighbour Luxembourg.

"I have many to thank, but I shall name one for all -- Jean-Claude Juncker," Kohl said, referring to Luxembourg's prime minister. Juncker had played a key role although many other smaller countries also supported Germany, he added.
Yet both Kohl and French president Jacques Chirac, clearly relieved that the Franco-German alliance had found its way back to consensus, stressed their cooperation was intact.
At his final news conference, Chirac termed the stability pact "a success for Franco-German cooperation".
Kohl saw the agreement as proof that "the Franco-German alliance works".

With financial markets conditioned by the months of hard bargaining to see a solid deal as an essential basis for a successful European currency, Kohl warned that the consequences of a failure could have been immense.
"What questions would you have posed if we had sat here in front of you and said we did not get an agreement?" he asked the assembled reporters.

But above all, the deal was important to reassure German citizens that the euro was a fair exchange for their cherished mark, which was important so that the higher political goals of European unity could be achieved, Kohl said.

"I am sure the majority of the German population think that they are paying a high price," for the European currency, he said, "But they will be prepared to pay that price if they know that as a result Europe can live in peace."
